sources.title: American Statistical Association releases statement on statistical significance and P-values: provides principles to improve the conduct and interpretation of quantitative science
sources.version: ASA news release of 7 March 2016 announcing the ASA Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values and reproducing its six principles in full. Companion article DOI 10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108
sources.locator: Page 2, numbered principles 1 (a p-value can indicate how incompatible the data are with a specified statistical model), 3 (conclusions should not be based only on whether a p-value passes a specific threshold), and 5 (a p-value, or statistical significance, does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result). Page 1 carries the executive director's remark about an arbitrary threshold.
sources.license: Copyright American Statistical Association; the release is distributed publicly by the association with no open-content reuse licence displayed, and no reuse licence is relied on here

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify that a professional statistical association has published, as formal principles, that a p-value indicates how incompatible data are with a specified statistical model, that neither a p-value nor statistical significance measures the size of an effect or the importance of a result, and that conclusions should not rest only on whether a p-value passes a threshold. No principle is quoted or reproduced. Each is restated in this lesson's own words and applied to invented teaching data, and none of the release's wording, list ordering, quotations or examples is reused.

agentAccess.notes: Route selection was made before substantive reading. The publisher route for the companion journal article, https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108, was excluded without being opened: that host's robots file carries an explicit record disallowing all paths to the named AI crawler GPTBot, which this project treats as a restriction on agent ingestion. The association's own distribution of the statement was used instead. https://www.amstat.org/robots.txt was requested on 2026-07-25 and returns HTTP 404, so the host publishes no robots file, declares no machine-readable crawler or text-mining directive, and exposes no terms page restricting automated reading. The three-page PDF was retrieved over plain HTTPS in a single request with no login, paywall, rate-limit breach or access-control bypass, and its text was read directly rather than through a search summary. This record covers the news release, which reproduces the six principles in full, and not the peer-reviewed article behind the excluded route.

sources.title: Statistical tests, P values, confidence intervals, and power: a guide to misinterpretations
sources.version: European Journal of Epidemiology volume 31, pages 337-350; DOI 10.1007/s10654-016-0149-3; PMCID PMC4877414
sources.locator: Section 'Common misinterpretations of single P values', numbered items 7 (significance indicating a substantively important relation, refuted by noting minor effects reach significance when a study is large) and 8 (lack of significance indicating a small effect, refuted by noting large effects are drowned in noise when a study is small). Also the guidance that interpretation demands the sizes of effect estimates and confidence limits, not merely whether P falls above or below 0.05.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify two facts about the behaviour of significance tests, that a large study can return a statistically significant test on a very minor effect and a small study can fail to detect a large one, and one recommendation, that interpretation should rest on the effect estimate and its confidence limits rather than on which side of a conventional cut-off a P value fell. No wording, numbered item, table, figure, worked example or organisational scheme is reproduced, adapted or closely paraphrased. Every study, number and case in this lesson is invented and the instructional sequence is original, so the article's CC BY licence is not relied on for any reuse.

sources.title: Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID) in Patient-Reported Outcome Measures for Neurological Conditions: Review of Concept and Methods
sources.publisher: Wolters Kluwer (Annals of Indian Academy of Neurology)
sources.version: Annals of Indian Academy of Neurology volume 26, issue 4, pages 334-343; DOI 10.4103/aian.aian_207_23; PMCID PMC10645230
sources.locator: Introduction, on a statistically significant change not being clinically relevant when the patient does not perceive it. Results, 'What is MCID?', for the definition as the smallest change patients perceive as beneficial and its 1989 introduction by Jaeschke and colleagues. Results, 'How to determine MCID?', for anchor-based against distribution-based methods and the absence of a gold standard. Results, 'Limitations of MCID', for values being dynamic and context-specific across populations.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the definition and origin of the minimal clinically important difference, the existence and character of the two families of estimation method, the absence of a gold-standard method, and the context and population dependence of the resulting thresholds. No wording, table, figure, instrument, worked estimate or organisational scheme from the review is reproduced, adapted or closely paraphrased, and no MCID value from any instrument it discusses is carried into this lesson. Every case and number here is invented for teaching, so the displayed non-commercial and share-alike terms are not relied on for any reuse.

sources.title: Beyond statistical significance: Embracing minimal clinically important difference for better patient care
sources.publisher: Baishideng Publishing Group (World Journal of Methodology)
sources.version: World Journal of Methodology volume 15, issue 1, article 97814; DOI 10.5662/wjm.v15.i1.97814; PMCID PMC11525893
sources.locator: Introduction, for the contrast between statistical significance and the smallest change a patient perceives as beneficial or detrimental, including a treatment reaching significance without meaningful benefit in daily life. Section 'Understanding MCID', for the definition and its introduction in the 1980s by Jaeschke, Singer and Guyatt. Calculation-methodology section, for anchor-based against distribution-based approaches and the point that the choice can change the value obtained.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to corroborate the definition and 1980s origin of the minimal clinically important difference, the two families of estimation method and their differing reference points, and the general point that a statistically significant treatment effect need not be one a patient experiences as beneficial. No wording, table, figure, example or organisational scheme is reproduced, adapted or closely paraphrased, and no numerical MCID value is taken from the article. All teaching material here is invented, so the displayed non-commercial terms are not relied on for any reuse.

agentAccess.notes: The PMC robots file was retrieved and read before substantive access. sources.title: Diabetes Tests & Diagnosis
creators: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
sources.publisher: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, National Institutes of Health
sources.locator: The fasting plasma glucose row of the diagnostic results table: 99 mg/dL or below indicates normal, 100 to 125 mg/dL indicates prediabetes, and 126 mg/dL or above indicates diabetes. The surrounding text supports the statement that a doctor usually uses a second test to confirm a diagnosis of diabetes, and the definition of fasting as having nothing to eat or drink except sips of water for at least eight hours before the test.
sources.license: US Government work; NIDDK content is published as a public service of the National Institutes of Health

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the three fasting plasma glucose diagnostic bands in mg/dL and the practice of confirming a diagnosis with a second test. These figures appear in this lesson to demonstrate that a diagnostic cut-point describes a level and cannot serve as an importance threshold for a change, which is a use the source does not itself make. No wording, table layout, illustration or patient-facing explanation from the page is reproduced or closely paraphrased.
